findings.what: teardown clears the process-wide incoming-call handler that AppDelegate installed once at launch: `if ([TGCall shared].onStateChanged != nil) [TGCall shared].onStateChanged = nil;` (teardown is called from viewWillDisappear:194 and dealloc:222).
findings.failure: AppDelegate.m:26 TGWatchForIncomingCalls() sets [TGCall shared].onStateChanged and is called exactly once, from application:didFinishLaunchingWithOptions: (AppDelegate.m:57). TGCallViewController.m:160 overwrites that same single-slot property with its own block, and teardown nils it. After the first call of any kind (incoming or outgoing) ends, [TGCall shared].onStateChanged is nil forever: a subsequent TGCallStatePending update fires no handler, so no incoming call screen is ever presented again for the rest of the process lifetime.
findings.fix: Make TGCallViewController save the previous handler before overwriting (`self.savedStateHandler = [TGCall shared].onStateChanged;` at line 160) and restore it in teardown instead of assigning nil, exactly as TGMediaViewController does for onFileProgress (TGMediaViewController.m:2199-2216). Better: expose TGWatchForIncomingCalls as a class method on AppDelegate and re-arm it from teardown.

findings.what: AVCaptureFileOutput's completion delegate does main-thread-only work on AVFoundation's private delegate queue: `- (void)captureOutput:...didFinishRecordingToOutputFileAtURL:...` calls `[self stopTimer]` (line 524 -> `[self.timer invalidate]` line 413) and `[self failWithCode:code]` (line 551 -> `[delegate videoRecorder:self didFailWithError:error]` line 104).
findings.failure: didFinishRecordingToOutputFileAtURL: is delivered on AVFoundation's internal serial queue, not the main queue. (a) NSTimer -invalidate must be sent from the thread that scheduled the timer (startTimer:405 schedules on the main run loop); invalidating from another thread leaves the timer firing against a torn-down recorder or over-releases it. (b) failWithCode: reaches TGVideoCaptureViewController.m:421 videoRecorder:didFailWithError:, which calls -resetToCamera and mutates UIKit views off the main thread - on iOS 6.1/armv7 this produces missing redraws, autolayout/CALayer corruption, and intermittent crashes when the user stops a too-short or failed recording. Note the success path (deliverFileAtPath:581) does hop to the main queue, so the failure path is inconsistent with the rest of the class.
findings.fix: Wrap the entire body of captureOutput:didFinishRecordingToOutputFileAtURL:fromConnections:error: (lines 523-555) in `dispatch_async(dispatch_get_main_queue(), ^{ ... })` with a `__weak typeof(self) weakSelf` guard, matching deliverFileAtPath:. Then stopTimer, discardOutputFile, failWithCode: and deliverFileAtPath: all run on main.

findings.what: Instant View block heights are measured on a background queue: `dispatch_async(dispatch_get_global_queue(...), ^{ ... [TGInstantViewController heightForBlock:block] ... })` (line 371-374), and heightForBlock: uses UIStringDrawing - `[caption sizeWithFont:[UIFont systemFontOfSize:13] constrainedToSize:... lineBreakMode:...]` (line 476) plus `+fontForKind:` (line 387).
findings.failure: NSString UIStringDrawing (-sizeWithFont:constrainedToSize:lineBreakMode:) is not thread-safe before iOS 7; the target here is iOS 6.1.3. Opening an Instant View article with captions/paragraphs measures dozens of strings concurrently with main-thread text drawing, which intermittently deadlocks or crashes inside the shared WebCore/CoreText font cache, and otherwise returns garbage heights that make rows overlap.
findings.fix: Do the measuring pass on the main queue: replace the global-queue dispatch at line 371 with a straight loop on main (heights are cheap - the article is at most a few hundred blocks), or precompute text sizes with CoreText (CTFramesetterSuggestFrameSizeWithConstraints), which is thread-safe on iOS 6, instead of -sizeWithFont:.

findings.what: A block-based notification observer is registered without keeping the token: `[[NSNotificationCenter defaultCenter] addObserverForName:TGThemeChangedNotification object:nil queue:[NSOperationQueue mainQueue] usingBlock:^(NSNotification *note){ ... }];` and dealloc (line 1688-1691) only does `[[NSNotificationCenter defaultCenter] removeObserver:self]`.
findings.failure: addObserverForName:... returns an opaque observer object which is what must be passed to removeObserver:; removeObserver:self does not unregister it. Every chat opened registers one more permanent observer that the notification center retains forever. On a theme change all of them fire: [TGIcons flush] runs once per chat ever opened, plus a reloadData against each dead controller's table via the weak reference. On a 512MB/40-60MB-usable iPhone 4S this is an unbounded observer + block leak and a visible stall on theme switch. TGChatListViewController.m:976 does this correctly (stores self.themeObserver and removes it in dealloc:1173) - this file simply dropped that.
findings.fix: Add `@property (nonatomic, strong) id themeObserver;` to the class extension, assign the return value at line 1432 (`self.themeObserver = [[NSNotificationCenter defaultCenter] addObserverForName:...]`), and in dealloc add `if (self.themeObserver) [[NSNotificationCenter defaultCenter] removeObserver:self.themeObserver];` before the existing removeObserver:self.

findings.what: TGMediaViewController save/restores the single global progress hook (`void (^previous)(NSInteger, float) = client.onFileProgress; self.savedProgressBlock = previous;` line 2199-2200, restored in removeProgressHook line 2214), but TGChatViewController.m:2338 overwrites the same property unconditionally (`[TGClient shared].onFileProgress = ^(NSInteger updatedId, float progress){ ... };`) and never restores or clears it.
findings.failure: Sequence: open a chat, tap a media file (beginDownloadHUD installs the chat's block at TGChatViewController.m:2338), open the media viewer (addProgressHook saves the chat block and chains), start another download from the chat (TGChatViewController.m:2338 replaces the chained block outright), close the media viewer -> removeProgressHook writes the stale saved block back over the chat's current one. The chat's download HUD freezes at whatever percentage it had reached and never updates, even though the download continues. The reverse order silently drops the media viewer's chaining.
findings.fix: Give TGClient a small array of progress observers (add/remove by token) instead of the single `onFileProgress` block, and convert both TGChatViewController.m:2338 and TGMediaViewController.m:2204 to register/unregister. Minimum fix: make TGChatViewController chain the same way the media viewer does (save the previous block in beginDownloadHUD, call it from inside the new block, restore it in endDownloadHUD at line 2347).

findings.what: `-request:completion:` stores the completion in self.pendingRequests (line 152) and only then calls -send:, which can silently drop the request: `NSData *data = [NSJSONSerialization dataWithJSONObject:request options:0 error:&err]; if (!data){ NSLog(@"TGClient: cannot encode %@: %@", request, err); return; }` (TGClient.m:116-121). There is also no timeout and no flush of pendingRequests on TDLib shutdown / logout.
findings.failure: Any request dictionary carrying a non-JSON value - an NSNull or NSDate that leaked out of a TDLib reply and was fed straight back in, an NSString built from invalid UTF-8, or a nil-boxed id - fails to encode. Nothing is ever sent, so no reply with that @extra ever arrives, so the completion sits in pendingRequests forever. Every caller that shows a spinner or HUD and hides it only in the completion (e.g. TGLoginViewController -setBusy:, TGMediaViewController download chrome) spins forever with no error path. The same happens for every in-flight request if TDLib is stopped, and the retained completions keep their captured controllers alive.
findings.fix: Make -send: report failure (`- (BOOL)send:`) and in -request:completion: remove the pending entry and invoke the completion with a synthetic error object (`@{@"@type": @"error", @"code": @(-1), @"message": @"encode failed"}`) when the send fails. Additionally, on shutdown/logout drain self.pendingRequests, calling each completion with the same synthetic error, and consider a per-request watchdog that fires the completion with an error after N seconds.

findings.what: The chat-action handler stored on the TGClient singleton captures a view strongly: `[TGClient shared].onChatAction = ^(int64_t chatId, NSString *action){ if (chatId != weakSelf.chatId) return; subtitle.text = action ?: restingSubtitle; };` - `subtitle` is the local UILabel created in -buildTitleView, and the block is never cleared (dealloc at line 1688 only invalidates the playback timer and removes NSNotificationCenter observers).
findings.failure: The singleton keeps the block, and the block keeps the subtitle UILabel of the last chat's title view alive for the rest of the process. Worse, the block keeps writing into a label belonging to a popped controller whenever a chat action update arrives for a chat whose id happens to match (weakSelf is nil after dealloc, so chatId != 0 usually short-circuits, but a chatId of 0 in a malformed update writes into the dead view).
findings.fix: Capture the label weakly (`__weak UILabel *weakSubtitle = subtitle;`) and resolve both weakSelf and weakSubtitle inside the block, bailing if either is nil; and clear `[TGClient shared].onChatAction = nil` in -dealloc (or better, set it in viewWillAppear alongside installMessageHandler and clear it in viewWillDisappear).
